title: Gibbs Variational Last Layers for Long-Horizon Dynamics Learning
claim: A family of training objectives builds incrementally from a simple baseline by adding multi-step structure, robust scoring, and autoregressive rollouts.
layout: 4 panels, left-to-right, curved arrows labeled with each loss extension
description: Four time-series panels run left to right, each showing a dashed dark-gray ground-truth trajectory with black dots on a light grid. The x-axis is Time T and the y-axis is X. Curved black arrows between panel titles carry the labels 'extension to multi-step', 'robust scoring' and 'autoregressive scoring'. They link the losses s-NLL, m-NLL, m-CRPS and m-arCRPS. Panel 1 (red) shows a single-step prediction with one uncertainty ellipse and the rest of the curve grayed out. Panel 2 (blue) shows several multi-step predictions with ellipses and a small inset parabola labeled e^2 over δ − δ̂. Panel 3 (orange and brown) shows robust predictions with a V-shaped |e| inset. Panel 4 (purple and pink) shows smooth autoregressive rollout trajectories with shaded uncertainty bands. Each panel has its own color, which marks the progression.
caption: Overview of the developed loss functions for VBLLs under the Gibbs VI framework. We extend existing single-step (\selbo) to a multi-step (\melbo), robust (\mfcrps), autoregressive loss (\marcrps).
abstract: Accurate long-horizon probabilistic predictions of dynamical systems are a prerequisite for model-based decision-making. Variational Bayesian last layers (VBLLs) are an attractive model class for this setting, offering tractable uncertainty at near-deterministic cost, yet they are trained exclusively with single-step likelihood objectives that may be insufficient for reliable multi-step rollouts. We revisit VBLLs through the lens of Gibbs variational inference, which decouples posterior inference from the choice of training loss. Building on this perspective, we introduce a family of multi-step training losses that progressively incorporate long-horizon structure, robustness via continuous ranked probability scores (CRPS), and training on full autoregressive rollouts. Our approach retains the simplicity of VBLLs while directly optimizing for multi-step predictive quality. Across illustrative synthetic environments, a diverse suite of chaotic dynamical systems, and real-world data, we show that multi-step, CRPS-based objectives substantially improve long-horizon accuracy and distributional fit, consistently outperforming single-step likelihood training.
